opencode_analysis.analysis:
False positive in practice: `result_path` is a pytest-generated JUnit report from the same CI job (`.github/scripts/run_integration_tests.py:400`), not untrusted external input; stdlib `ElementTree` doesn't resolve external entities, and attacker-controlled code in that job already has execution.

Settle it with a test that runs `_sanitize_and_load_junit` on a handcrafted `.xml` containing `<!DOCTYPE ... [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]>` and a billion-laughs payload, asserting no file contents appear and it fails fast (`ValueError`/`ParseError` path).

If you want defense-in-depth, swapping to `defusedxml.ElementTree` is a one-line change.

False positive for the security rule: MD5 is used at service.py:1825 only as a 7-char non-cryptographic fingerprint to shorten long URLs in LLM prompts, not for authentication or signatures, so collision resistance is irrelevant here. The only theoretical concern is a 28-bit hash collision mapping a shortened URL to the wrong original, but that is a robustness nit, not an exploitable vulnerability. A unit test calling `_replace_urls_in_text` with two long URLs sharing the truncated prefix but differing tails, then asserting each shortened form resolves to its own original, settles it. Verdict: false positive (not worth maintainer time).

**False positive.** `python/conftest.py:36` hashes OpenAI request bodies (`model`/`messages`/`tools`) solely for VCR cassette matching; the other MD5 at line 119 hashes pytest node IDs for temp paths. Neither is a signature, secret, or security boundary — an MD5 collision would at worst match the wrong test cassette. No fix needed beyond, optionally, swapping in SHA-256 to silence scanners. Settling test: a unit test calling `custom_request_matcher` on two equivalent request bodies (and one differing body) to prove the hash is only a lookup key; run via `TEST=tests/integration_tests/wrappers/test_gemini.py make tests` for cassette replay.
